name: How to Evaluate a Home Addition Proposal in Los Angeles County

mainEntity.name: What should homeowners in Los Angeles County look for in a contractor’s home addition proposal beyond the price per square foot?
mainEntity.text: What should homeowners in Los Angeles County look for in a contractor’s home addition proposal beyond the price per square foot?

acceptedAnswer.text: Relying on a single “price per square foot” to choose a contractor for a home addition in Los Angeles County is risky. A thorough proposal should clearly describe the scope of work, including demolition, structural changes, exterior finishes, interior finishes, and any site work or utility upgrades. Verify whether design and engineering are included or if you must hire a separate architect or engineer. Look closely at exclusions and allowances. Exclusions outline what the contractor will not provide, such as landscaping, custom closets, or appliance installation. Allowances set placeholder budgets for items like tile, fixtures, or cabinets; low allowances can make a bid appear cheaper but lead to large upcharges once you select real products. The proposal should also spell out who is responsible for permit submittal, corrections, and inspection scheduling. A realistic schedule with major milestones, clear payment terms tied to progress, and a defined change order process are essential. You want to know how unexpected conditions will be priced and approved. Finally, review warranty terms and post-completion support. In a competitive market like Los Angeles County, selecting a contractor with a transparent, detailed proposal—and a track record of similar additions—often saves money and stress compared to choosing solely on headline price.
acceptedAnswer.description: Homeowners in Los Angeles County should look beyond price per square foot and compare scope details, exclusions, allowances, schedule, permit responsibilities, change order policies, payment milestones, and warranty terms. A complete proposal clearly defines what is included, how unforeseen conditions are handled, and who manages design, engineering, and inspections.
